summary.text: A galaxy cluster is a structure of hundreds to thousands of galaxies held together by gravity.
Clusters consist of galaxies, heated gas and dark matter, and they are the biggest known gravitationally bound structures in the universe.
Galaxies make up only a small fraction of a cluster, while dark matter makes up most of its mass and cannot be detected optically.

facts.label: Galaxy count
facts.value: Hundreds to thousands, bound by gravity

facts.label: Hot gas
facts.value: Peaks at 30 to 100 million degrees Celsius

items.prompt: You weigh a galaxy cluster by its gravity. Which of its components accounts for most of the mass?

options.label: The galaxies you can see in a photograph
The heated gas between the galaxies
Dark matter, which cannot be detected optically
The stars at the cluster's center

items.explain: Dark matter makes up the majority of a cluster's mass, while galaxies are only a small fraction.

items.prompt: As a cluster forms, gas collides with existing material. What does that do to the gas?

options.label: It heats it to tens of millions of degrees, giving X-rays
It cools it down into a dense cloud of new stars
It pushes all of it out past the cluster's edge
It slowly turns it into invisible dark matter

items.explain: Gas colliding with existing material generates shock waves that heat it to tens of millions of degrees and produce X-ray emission.

items.prompt: A cluster sits in front of a very distant, faint galaxy. How can it help telescopes see that galaxy?

options.label: Its hot gas brightens the faint galaxy behind it
Its galaxies act as relay stations for the light
Its dark matter absorbs any unwanted glare
Its gravity bends the light's path, like a magnifying glass

items.explain: Gravitational lensing by massive clusters bends the path of photons into a cosmic magnifying glass, revealing distant galaxies.

items.prompt: Astronomers find a small gathering of galaxies. What do they call it?

options.label: A supercluster, since it holds several galaxies
A galaxy group, since only larger aggregates count as clusters
A protocluster, since it is still forming
A galaxy cluster, since any gathering counts

items.explain: Small aggregates are called galaxy groups rather than clusters, and groups and clusters together form superclusters.

items.prompt: Two photons leave a cluster, one from its middle and one from its edge. Which loses more energy escaping, and why?

options.label: The edge one, since it travels farther
They lose the same, since they leave together
The central one, since gravity is stronger at the center
The central one, since the gas is thinner

items.explain: Photons from the center of a cluster lose more energy than those from the edge because gravity is stronger in the center.

items.prompt: What separates a protocluster from a finished galaxy cluster?

options.label: It has not yet collapsed into a bound cluster
It holds no galaxies inside it at all
It contains no gas of any kind
It has no dark matter in it at all

items.explain: Protoclusters are massive concentrations of plasma gas where galaxies are still forming and which have yet to collapse into a bound cluster.

paragraphs.heading: Giant families of galaxies
paragraphs.text: A galaxy cluster is a gathering of hundreds to thousands of galaxies held together by gravity. A typical cluster has a mass of 10¹⁴ to 10¹⁵ times that of the Sun. Clusters are made of galaxies, hot gas and dark matter. They are the largest structures in the universe known to be bound by gravity, and until superclusters were found in the 1980s they were thought to be the largest structures of all.

paragraphs.heading: Groups, clusters and superclusters
paragraphs.text: Smaller collections of galaxies are called galaxy groups rather than clusters. Groups and clusters together make up superclusters. A typical cluster is 1 to 5 Mpc, or megaparsecs, across. Its galaxies move at a spread of speeds of roughly 800 to 1000 km/s.

paragraphs.heading: Three ingredients
paragraphs.text: A cluster has three main parts. The galaxies are the only part we can see in visible light, yet they are only a small share of the cluster. The gas between them, called the intracluster medium, reaches peak temperatures of 30 to 100 million degrees Celsius. Dark matter makes up most of the mass, but it cannot be seen with optical telescopes.

paragraphs.heading: How clusters grow
paragraphs.text: Clusters start out as protoclusters: big concentrations of plasma gas where galaxies are still forming and nothing has yet collapsed into a bound cluster. As a cluster forms, it releases huge amounts of energy. Gas crashes into material already there, making shock waves that heat it to tens of millions of degrees so that it gives off X-rays. Inside the finished cluster, galaxies change through encounters such as mergers and through having their gas stripped away.

paragraphs.heading: A test of general relativity
paragraphs.text: Radek Wojtak used clusters to test a prediction of general relativity: light escaping a gravitational field loses energy. Gravity is stronger at a cluster's centre, so light from there should arrive with a longer wavelength than light from the edge. This effect is called gravitational redshift. Using data from 8000 clusters, Wojtak found the redshift grew with distance from the centre, just as general relativity predicts.

paragraphs.heading: Nature's magnifying glass
paragraphs.text: A cluster's mass warps space-time around it and bends the paths of passing light. That turns the cluster into a cosmic magnifying glass, known as a gravitational lens. Telescopes can use it to see distant galaxies in their early stages that could not otherwise be detected. In one case, astronomers used the Phoenix cluster to study a dwarf galaxy in an early, high-energy phase of star formation.

paragraphs.heading: Famous examples
paragraphs.text: Well-known clusters fairly near us include the Virgo, Fornax, Hercules and Coma clusters. A huge gathering of galaxies called the Great Attractor, dominated by the Norma Cluster, has enough mass to affect how the universe expands in our neighbourhood. Much farther away, SPT-CL J0546-5345 and SPT-CL J2106-5844 are the most massive clusters found in the early universe.
